messages.subject: Model adjustments and confidence intervals questions
messages.subject_clean: Model adjustments and confidence intervals questions
messages.body_plain:
1) I am attempting to redo my detection function plots using statistical
software (S-Plus), but when I try to recreate the model, I am missing the
adjustments.  For example, I know the equation for the half-normal model,
and according to Distance the best fit for my data had three cosine
adjustment terms.  In order for me to plot this model in S-Plus, what are
the adjustment equations and how do they fit into the original formula for
the model?  Distance gives the point estimates for the parameters, but I
don't understand how to recreate the detection function curve.

2)  My confidence intervals, as produce by Distance, are not even - does
Distance transform the data (using a Z-statistic or some other method), and
if so, how?

Please feel free to reply to the list or me personally
(ke...@zoology.ubc.ca).
Thank you,
Alison

Distance is intended to be used in conjunction with the book 'Introduction
to Distance Sampling', published by OUP, or its predecessor, which is on
our web pages at http://www.ruwpa.st-and.ac.uk/distancebook/.  The formula
is given there.  (e.g. p59 of the OUP book.)

> > 2)  My confidence intervals, as produce by Distance, are not even - does
> > Distance transform the data (using a Z-statistic or some other method), and
> > if so, how?

Again, this is covered in the book.  Unless you select the bootstrap, a
log-normal distribution is assumed.  See p77 of the OUP book.

messages.subject: recaps within lines
messages.body_plain:
I conducted a distance-sampling survey of desert tortoises this survey using
1-km transects laid out in a 250-m square. Sometimes we were unable to
complete a transect (e.g., we would complete 2 or 3 sides of the square),
and we would come back to finish it on another day. On 1 occasion we
recaptured a tortoise on a different side of the transect than it was marked
previously. My question is this: should I discard the second observation of
this individual tortoise, since it was observed on the same line (even
though on different days)?  We surveyed a total of 108.25 km and encountered
38 tortoises, not counting the recapture.

Thanks for any advice,

Roy Averill-Murray
Averill...@msn.com

messages.subject: Re: recaps within lines
messages.body_plain:
> > I conducted a distance-sampling survey of desert tortoises this survey using
> > 1-km transects laid out in a 250-m square. Sometimes we were unable to
> > complete a transect (e.g., we would complete 2 or 3 sides of the square),
> > and we would come back to finish it on another day. On 1 occasion we
> > recaptured a tortoise on a different side of the transect than it was marked
> > previously. My question is this: should I discard the second observation of
> > this individual tortoise, since it was observed on the same line (even
> > though on different days)?  We surveyed a total of 108.25 km and encountered
> > 38 tortoises, not counting the recapture.

I would include it if it had moved to a section of line you hadn't covered
at the previous visit.  This is because on average you would expect as
many tortoises to go the other way - i.e. ones that you would have
detected at the first visit had you carried on but missed because they had
moved to a section of line covered on your first visit.  (Similarly,
tortoises that moved out of detection range between visits will on average
be balanced by ones that move in.)  The principle is that you're getting a
snapshot estimate of density along the lines.  If you omit this tortoise,
you're getting a downward biased estimate of the snapshot density along
the section of line covered on the second visit.

Steve Buckland

messages.subject: Survey design: repeated tracklines or new ones?
messages.subject_clean: Survey design: repeated tracklines or new ones?
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I have just read the excellent section on survey design in the new book on
Distance Sampling. I am still unclear on one thing though, and wondered if
any list members had any thoughts on this.

I am helping to design an aerial survey of blue whales, to take place over
two years, with one survey per month. Encounter rate is expected to be
low, and highly variable according to the migration season. The objective
is to obtain estimates of absolute abundance, according to time of
year. Clearly there will be lots of g(0)-related difficulties, but in
terms of trackline design, is there anything to be gained by setting new
'random' (systematic with random startpoint) tracklines each month? My
feeling is no, there isn't, but am I missing something?

Thanks in advance for any help/advice on this issue.

Sharon.

messages.subject: Re: Survey design: repeated tracklines or new ones?
messages.subject_clean: Survey design: repeated tracklines or new ones?
messages.body_plain:
> > I am helping to design an aerial survey of blue whales, to take place over
> > two years, with one survey per month. Encounter rate is expected to be
> > low, and highly variable according to the migration season. The objective
> > is to obtain estimates of absolute abundance, according to time of
> > year. Clearly there will be lots of g(0)-related difficulties, but in
> > terms of trackline design, is there anything to be gained by setting new
> > 'random' (systematic with random startpoint) tracklines each month? My
> > feeling is no, there isn't, but am I missing something?

For terrestrial surveys, we would advocate repeating the same lines at
each visit if the main purpose is to estimate trend over time, but
covering new lines each time if the main purpose is to obtain a precise
estimate of average abundance over the time period.  In both cases, the
justification is that it gives you better precision for estimating the
quantity of interest.  These arguments also apply for marine surveys,
although marine habitats and animals tend to be more mobile, so the
arguments are less compelling.  However, if the overriding objective is an
estimate of average abundance over the period of the survey, I would
favour different tracklines in each survey, as this will ensure that
favoured localities are sampled in proportion.  (If you use the same lines
every time, and the number of lines is not large, then if you by chance
sample a high density area, you will sample it in every
survey;  conversely if you miss it, you will miss it in every survey.)

Steve

messages.subject: Replicates or not
messages.body_plain:
We've competed a pilot line transect survey for estimating black rockfish
density using scuba along a 25.3 mile section of coast line of the northern
Gulf of Alaska.  This was a first year pilot study so I hoped to gain enough
data to design a survey for next summer.   Fish density was assumed to
change with depth so the transect lines were aligned perpendicular to the
shoreline (running from 0 feet to about 80 feet).  Lines were laid out
systematically with a random starting point.  Line spacing was 1.1 nautical
miles as measured along the contour of the shoreline (total number of
samples K = 23).  A diver ran down transect line (l_i) from 0 to 80 feet and
stopped counting fish.  He than swam along the depth contour for greater
than double the maximum visibility.  The diver than ran a new transect line
from 80 to 0 feet.  My thought was that I would end up with two estimates of
fish density (though not independent) from the same area (e.g., Survey 1
would constitute all the 0 to 80 foot transect legs [k=23], and Survey 2
would constitute all the 80 to 0 foot transect legs [k=23]).  My question is
whether it is valid to pool - what I'm calling - Survey 1 with Survey 2.
Transect legs (l_i) are replicate samples of L and are chosen in either say
a random or system manner.  My 0 to 80 foot and 80 to 0 foot legs are not
independent samples and it seems to me that pooling the data would be
invalid.  On the other hand I sort of have replicates within replicates,
which doesn't seem like such a bad thing.  Any thoughts?
Many thanks, Mike

> > density using scuba along a 25.3 mile section of coast line of the northern
> > Gulf of Alaska.  This was a first year pilot study so I hoped to gain enough
> > data to design a survey for next summer.   Fish density was assumed to

> > miles as measured along the contour of the shoreline (total number of
> > samples K = 23).  A diver ran down transect line (l_i) from 0 to 80 feet and
> > stopped counting fish.  He than swam along the depth contour for greater
> > than double the maximum visibility.  The diver than ran a new transect line
> > from 80 to 0 feet.  My thought was that I would end up with two estimates of
> > fish density (though not independent) from the same area (e.g., Survey 1
> > would constitute all the 0 to 80 foot transect legs [k=23], and Survey 2
> > would constitute all the 80 to 0 foot transect legs [k=23]).  My question is
> > whether it is valid to pool - what I'm calling - Survey 1 with Survey 2.
> > Transect legs (l_i) are replicate samples of L and are chosen in either say
> > a random or system manner.  My 0 to 80 foot and 80 to 0 foot legs are not
> > independent samples and it seems to me that pooling the data would be
> > invalid.  On the other hand I sort of have replicates within replicates,
> > which doesn't seem like such a bad thing.  Any thoughts?

Mike, you are better to pool for the very reason that they aren't
independent!  For a single transect, pool the sightings data from the
outward and return legs, and record effort as twice the line length.  When
we estimate variance in encounter rate, we assume independence AMONG
lines, not independence of detections WITHIN lines.  Also, if you use the
bootstrap to quantify precision, by resampling lines, then independence of
detections within a single line is not required for any of the components
of the density estimate.  These issues are covered in the Distance
Sampling books - e.g. p294 of the 2001 book.

Steve Buckland
